title: Worst-Case Quantum Algorithm for Optimal Polynomial Intersection Beyond Decoded Quantum Interferometry
abstract: The Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem asks us to find a low-degree polynomial over a finite field whose values lie in prescribed subsets on as many given inputs as possible. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) gives a quantum algorithm for OPI in parameter regimes beyond those achieved by the best known classical heuristics. Follow-up works improve the parameter regimes, but their analyses are limited to average-case settings. Recently, Sun and Wootters showed that, even in the worst case, OPI has a solution in a larger parameter regime than the one covered by DQI. However, they left open whether one can design a quantum algorithm that solves OPI in the worst-case beyond the DQI regime.   We give such a quantum algorithm. As a byproduct, we also improve the existential bound of Sun and Wootters in certain parameter regimes. In particular, when each subset contains roughly half of the field elements, our algorithm finds a solution with satisfaction rate $s=1$ whenever the rate satisfies $R>0.75$. This matches the previous average-case bound, whereas DQI cannot achieve $s=1$ unless $R=1$. Our existential bound guarantees the existence of a solution when $R> 0.7158$, improving over the previous threshold $R>0.7495$. More generally, our existential results extend to the Max-LINSAT problem with respect to arbitrary maximum distance separable (MDS) codes. The corresponding algorithmic results apply only to MDS codes whose dual admits an efficient list decoder. Our results are obtained through a novel application of a Brascamp--Lieb-type inequality in the MDS setting, which may have further applications.
summary: This paper develops a new worst-case quantum algorithm for solving the Optimal Polynomial Intersection problem. It significantly improves upon prior theoretical bounds by achieving high satisfaction rates ($s=1$) in regimes previously unreachable by DQI, particularly when analyzing MDS codes. The work advances the understanding of quantum computational limits for structured algebraic problems.
main_problem: The paper addresses the Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, which seeks to find a low-degree polynomial satisfying membership constraints on many inputs.
main_result: The authors present a novel quantum algorithm that solves OPI in the worst-case regime beyond what is achievable by Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI).
method: The core methodology involves applying a novel application of a Brascamp--Lieb-type inequality within the framework of Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes.
model_or_system: The problem is framed abstractly over finite fields ($\mathbb{F}_q$) and relies on quantum oracle access to membership information for prescribed subsets $\{S_i\}$.
key_observables: Satisfaction rate ($s$), the ratio parameter $R=k/n$, and the existence threshold for a solution.
important_parameters: The density $ho = |S_i|/q$ is crucial, with specific focus on the balanced case $ho=1/2$.
main_assumptions: General algorithmic results are restricted to MDS codes whose dual admits an efficient list decoder; initial guarantees were based on random choices of sets.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares achievable satisfaction rates ($s$) for DQI, average-case bounds, and the new worst-case algorithm in the balanced case. Figure 2 and Figure 3 compare saturation/satisfaction bounds across different regimes.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing the OPI problem definition to comparing algorithmic bounds against prior work (DQI, average-case). It then develops the novel quantum algorithm using advanced inequalities in the MDS setting, culminating in improved worst-case and existential bounds for OPI and MaxLINSAT.
why_interesting: While highly abstract, the techniques involving quantum algorithms to solve hard combinatorial/coding theory problems (like list decoding or polynomial intersection) are foundational to understanding the limits of quantum computation for structured data processing.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison of achievable algorithmic satisfaction rates in the balanced case ρ = 1/2.

Figure 2: Comparison of algorithmic saturation bounds as functions of ρ. The direct application of Theorem 6.1 yields a non-monotone curve, with a bump for ρ > 0.5200. This bump is only an artifact of the proof. Indeed, by a simple thinning argument (see Lemma A.1), we may replace the sets by smaller subsets, and hence replace ρ by a smaller value, without reducing the target satisfaction rate. Thus, for ρ > 0.5200, we use the horizontal bound obtained by applying Theo- rem 6.1 at ρ ≈0.5200, wherever this improves upon the bound obtained from a direct application of Theorem 6.1 at the actual value of ρ.
Figure 3: Comparison of existential satisfaction rates in the balanced case ρ = 1/2.

Figure 4: Comparison of existential saturation bounds as functions of ρ. The Sun–Wootters curve is based on [SW26, Theorems 1.6 and 1.9]. While [SW26, Theorem 1.9] gives a bound for general ρ, it has a bump for ρ > 1/2. On the other hand, [SW26, Theorem 1.6] gives a better bound in the balanced case ρ ≈1/2. By a thinning argument similar to the one discussed in Appendix A, one can increase the density ρ without sacrificing the satisfaction rate. Thus, in the regime ρ ≥1/2, whenever the bound from [SW26, Theorem 1.9] is worse, we plot the thinned balanced-case bound, which gives R ≈0.7495.
